bull_bear.body:
- Long-standing execution track record in urban infrastructure, industrial parks, environmental infrastructure and particularly water and wastewater management — areas where the Managing Director states execution experience matters and has been built over many years

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Single-activity and single-sector concentration — 100% of turnover is construction — BRSR Section A reports one main activity (construction: EPC, O&M of infrastructure development projects in buildings, industrial, water and wastewater, and roads & bridges) contributing 100% of turnover, under NIC codes 41001/41002/41003/42101/42203/42204/42205. There is no diversifying revenue stream, so an infrastructure-ordering slowdown transmits directly to the whole business.
- Government and public-sector client concentration — BRSR states both the Developer and the EPC businesses are primarily associated with government-led projects and contracts awarded by government authorities and related agencies. Revenue, receivable collection and payment timing therefore depend on public budgets, tendering cycles and authority behaviour rather than on a diversified private customer base.
- Counterparty / concession-authority disputes and receivable recoverability — The Directors' Report records that receivables of INR 724.28 million (standalone) and INR 807.71 million (consolidated) were written off in FY 2025-26 as long outstanding balances no longer recoverable. Separately, NHAI deducted INR 2,509.46 million from annuities payable to subsidiary Srinagar Banihal Expressway Limited; the Independent Engineer has recommended release of INR 1,872.75 million and SBEL has initiated arbitration, but the outcome is presently unascertainable and no adjustment has been made in the financial statements.
- Project-specific-entity termination risk in the developer/concession portfolio — The auditors drew attention to the mutual-consent termination by NHAI and subsidiary Hospet Chitradurga Tollways Limited of that concession. Because HCTL is a project-specific company, termination affected its going-concern status and its accounts were prepared on a realisation basis. This is the structural fragility of single-asset SPVs in the developer portfolio.
- Insolvency proceedings brought by operational creditors — As at 31 March 2026 a cumulative four applications had been filed by operational creditors against the Company under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 before the NCLT, with one operational creditor having appealed to NCLAT, Chennai Bench. The report states none had been admitted and there was no change in status post 31 March 2026, but pending applications remain a live contingency.
- Legal and regulatory compliance risk — The BRSR material-issues table identifies legal & regulatory compliance as a risk with negative implications: non-compliance with applicable laws and regulations may result in penalties, legal action, reputational damage and disruption to business operations. The Secretarial Auditor observed statutory forms filed with the Registrar of Companies beyond prescribed timelines, a delayed filing of the AGM outcome with the stock exchange, and a delayed submission of Integrated Financial Results to NSE for which a penalty was paid — evidence that the risk has crystallised in small ways during the year.
- Execution dependence on people and on third-party contractors — The BRSR identifies employee attraction, training and engagement as material to effective project execution, and turnover of permanent employees rose to 28.33% in FY 2025-26 from 17.73% in FY 2024-25. The Company also states it does not employ workers directly: project execution is carried out through third-party contractors who manage their own workforce, so site delivery quality, safety and labour compliance depend on subcontractor performance.
- Working capital intensity and lengthening receivable cycle — Debtors turnover lengthened to 146 days in FY 2025-26 from 110 days in FY 2024-25, a 33% increase which the Company attributes to the decrease in revenue during the year. Management identifies strengthening cash conversion and deepening working capital discipline as core priorities, and the Company continues to rely on working capital facilities and guarantee/surety instruments to service contracts.
- Data privacy and cyber exposure as operations digitise — The BRSR material-issues table notes that Ramky's operations increasingly rely on digital platforms and stakeholder data (employees, customers and vendors), that responsible data handling supports compliance with evolving regulations such as India's DPDP Act, and that it affects eligibility for large infrastructure projects with stringent IT and governance requirements.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Selective growth: pursue only those projects and partnerships where Ramky has the capabilities to execute well, where the commercial proposition is sound and where long-term value can be created — the CEO states the growth strategy will remain selective and the MD that the company is becoming more selective and more focused
- Anchor the portfolio on water and wastewater, industrial parks and urban/environmental infrastructure, where the MD says execution experience matters and Ramky has built that experience over many years
- Combine organic growth with inorganic expansion — evaluate strategic partnerships and acquisitions that add capabilities, strengthen market position and complement existing businesses
- Professionalise the organisation: bring in experienced professionals and industry specialists with deep domain knowledge, adopt more professional processes, and bring greater focus to performance and accountability
- Strengthen R&D and compliance capabilities to support the industries developing around the infrastructure ecosystems
- Strengthen cash conversion and deepen working capital discipline, evaluating every opportunity through the lens of risk-adjusted returns and deploying capital with intent and precision
- Maintain an agile treasury function that widens access to low-cost funds and structures project-specific financing matched to the risk and return profile of each opportunity, including insurance surety bonds as an alternative to conventional bank guarantees
- Use structured exits and restructuring where they help sharpen focus and unlock value, supported by an annual strategic planning process keeping capital, risk and growth priorities aligned
- Operate across a balanced mix of EPC, development and long-term operating opportunities, participating across the infrastructure lifecycle from development and construction to commissioning and long-term operations

outlook.body: Ramky's FY26 expansion is order-book driven rather than plant-capex driven: the Company added three large awards across its EPC and developer portfolio — a water transmission project from the Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board, the Dighi Port Industrial Area Phase 1 (Package A) infrastructure works from Maharashtra Industrial Township Limited, and a Life Sciences City project from the Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation. The Dighi Port Phase 1 award is an EPC contract for design, construction, testing, commissioning, operation and maintenance of infrastructure works under the Delhi Mumbai Industrial Corridor, with an awarded contract value of ₹1,400 crore, a 930-day construction period spanning five milestones from design to completion, and a four-year defect liability period. Alongside it, Ramky and MIDC are developing MILéS City, a 1,000-hectare integrated life sciences ecosystem in the Dighi Port Industrial Area comprising a 607.70 ha industrial zone, 125.54 ha of green spaces, 113.12 ha of roads and parking, 62.62 ha of common amenities, 51.33 ha of utilities and a 39.69 ha commercial zone, planned with an all-weather road network, GIS substation and power distribution, a common effluent treatment plant with ZLD facility, a dedicated co-generation power plant with steam distribution, hazardous waste management, a water treatment plant with distribution network, warehousing, an integrated command control centre and R&D, skill-development and emergency-response facilities. In water, the Godavari Drinking Water Supply Scheme Phase II & III Package II is being executed under the Hybrid Annuity Model over a two-year construction period followed by ten years of operation and maintenance, and comprises 65 km of 2,200 mm-dia raw-water main from Ghanpur to Osmansagar and Himayatsagar, 42 km of 2,400 mm-dia clear-water main from Ghanpur to Muthangi, water treatment plants of 120 MLD at Osmansagar and 70 MLD at Himayatsagar, and master balancing reservoirs of 102.5 ML combined capacity at Ghanpur and Golden Mile, supporting Hyderabad's water infrastructure and the Musi River rejuvenation. At V.O. Chidambaranar Port a Ramky JV is developing a 3 MLD seawater reverse-osmosis desalination plant on a Design-Build-Operate model with a 450 mm seawater intake pipeline and a 250 mm discharge pipeline, with the JV responsible for five years of operation and maintenance after commissioning. Structurally, the Company also consolidated its group: the NCLT Hyderabad Bench-II order dated 25 February 2026 approved the amalgamation of Sehore Kosmi Tollways Limited and Ramky Elsamex Hyderabad Ring Road Limited into Ramky Infrastructure Limited, and the assets and liabilities of the transferor companies have been vested in the Company. Management states it is also evaluating strategic partnerships and acquisitions that can add capabilities and expand the portfolio.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's infrastructure requirements are changing — rapid urbanisation, growing industrial activity, water stress and increasing environmental requirements are creating a larger need for sustainable infrastructure solutions, which the MD says positions Ramky to participate in this growth particularly in water, wastewater and environmental infrastructure
- Sustained public capital expenditure remains central to India's growth: the Union Budget 2025-26 provided ₹11.21 lakh crore for capital expenditure (3.1% of GDP) and effective capital expenditure of ₹15.48 lakh crore (4.3% of GDP), with government capital outlay up nearly 89% from ₹5.92 lakh crore in FY2021-22
- Real GDP is estimated to grow 7.4% in FY2025-26 and construction GVA 7.8%, per the First Advance Estimates of the National Statistical Office
- The infrastructure opportunity is shifting from creating basic infrastructure to improving quality, capacity and efficiency of existing systems, and increasingly toward projects that combine construction with long-term operation, maintenance, resource efficiency and measurable outcomes — a structure that favours Ramky's EPC-plus-O&M model
- Water and wastewater demand driver: India generates approximately 112 billion litres of domestic and industrial wastewater daily, the world's third-largest, with urban areas about two-thirds of the volume and only 28% of urban wastewater currently treated
- Reuse of treated water for industrial cooling, construction and landscaping is estimated by the Economic Survey to represent an economic opportunity of ₹2.4-3.2 lakh crore by 2047, with the sector moving toward reuse, resource recovery, pollution control and circular water management
- Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0, approved in March 2026, extends the mission to December 2028 with an enhanced outlay of ₹8.69 lakh crore, emphasising reliable and sustainable drinking-water services; AMRUT 2.0 continues to support urban water supply, sewerage, septage management and water-body rejuvenation
- Performance-linked models such as Hybrid Annuity Models for sewage treatment are supporting the transition and align with Ramky's HAM capability
- Industrial parks: the sector grew 8.4% in the first half of FY2025-26; the Government's BHAVYA scheme approved in March 2026 provides for 100 plug-and-play industrial parks with ready infrastructure, driving demand for supporting utilities, water supply, wastewater treatment and common facilities
- Roads, bridges and transportation infrastructure continues to benefit from sustained public investment aimed at improving connectivity and reducing logistics costs
- PM GatiShakti continues to improve integrated planning and coordination across infrastructure projects, while continued EPC, PPP and hybrid-model private investment is creating new opportunities across transportation, urban infrastructure, water and industrial development
- The CFO states the Company enters the new financial year with real momentum and a business pipeline stronger than it has ever been
- The CFO states the order book stands at approximately INR 13,000 Crores, describing it as a signal of continued client trust
- FY26 wins cited as milestones: the INR 2,085 Crore water transmission project awarded by the Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board; the INR 1,401 Crore infrastructure works at Dighi Port Industrial Area awarded by Maharashtra Industrial Township Limited; and the INR 3,000 Crore Life Sciences City project awarded by the Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation
- The BRSR director's statement describes significant business momentum with several project wins across the EPC and developer portfolio, including HMWSSB Water Transmission in Telangana, Dighi Port Industrial Area Phase I in Maharashtra (MITL) and the 1,000-hectare Life Sciences park from MIDC

risks.risk: Single-activity and single-sector concentration — 100% of turnover is construction
risks.note: BRSR Section A reports one main activity (construction: EPC, O&M of infrastructure development projects in buildings, industrial, water and wastewater, and roads & bridges) contributing 100% of turnover, under NIC codes 41001/41002/41003/42101/42203/42204/42205. There is no diversifying revenue stream, so an infrastructure-ordering slowdown transmits directly to the whole business.

BRSR states both the Developer and the EPC businesses are primarily associated with government-led projects and contracts awarded by government authorities and related agencies. Revenue, receivable collection and payment timing therefore depend on public budgets, tendering cycles and authority behaviour rather than on a diversified private customer base.

risks.risk: Counterparty / concession-authority disputes and receivable recoverability
risks.note: The Directors' Report records that receivables of INR 724.28 million (standalone) and INR 807.71 million (consolidated) were written off in FY 2025-26 as long outstanding balances no longer recoverable. Separately, NHAI deducted INR 2,509.46 million from annuities payable to subsidiary Srinagar Banihal Expressway Limited; the Independent Engineer has recommended release of INR 1,872.75 million and SBEL has initiated arbitration, but the outcome is presently unascertainable and no adjustment has been made in the financial statements.

risks.risk: Project-specific-entity termination risk in the developer/concession portfolio
risks.note: The auditors drew attention to the mutual-consent termination by NHAI and subsidiary Hospet Chitradurga Tollways Limited of that concession. Because HCTL is a project-specific company, termination affected its going-concern status and its accounts were prepared on a realisation basis. This is the structural fragility of single-asset SPVs in the developer portfolio.

risks.risk: Insolvency proceedings brought by operational creditors
risks.note: As at 31 March 2026 a cumulative four applications had been filed by operational creditors against the Company under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 before the NCLT, with one operational creditor having appealed to NCLAT, Chennai Bench. The report states none had been admitted and there was no change in status post 31 March 2026, but pending applications remain a live contingency.

The BRSR material-issues table identifies legal & regulatory compliance as a risk with negative implications: non-compliance with applicable laws and regulations may result in penalties, legal action, reputational damage and disruption to business operations. The Secretarial Auditor observed statutory forms filed with the Registrar of Companies beyond prescribed timelines, a delayed filing of the AGM outcome with the stock exchange, and a delayed submission of Integrated Financial Results to NSE for which a penalty was paid — evidence that the risk has crystallised in small ways during the year.

risks.risk: Execution dependence on people and on third-party contractors
risks.note: The BRSR identifies employee attraction, training and engagement as material to effective project execution, and turnover of permanent employees rose to 28.33% in FY 2025-26 from 17.73% in FY 2024-25. The Company also states it does not employ workers directly: project execution is carried out through third-party contractors who manage their own workforce, so site delivery quality, safety and labour compliance depend on subcontractor performance.

risks.risk: Working capital intensity and lengthening receivable cycle
risks.note: Debtors turnover lengthened to 146 days in FY 2025-26 from 110 days in FY 2024-25, a 33% increase which the Company attributes to the decrease in revenue during the year. Management identifies strengthening cash conversion and deepening working capital discipline as core priorities, and the Company continues to rely on working capital facilities and guarantee/surety instruments to service contracts.

risks.risk: Data privacy and cyber exposure as operations digitise
risks.note: The BRSR material-issues table notes that Ramky's operations increasingly rely on digital platforms and stakeholder data (employees, customers and vendors), that responsible data handling supports compliance with evolving regulations such as India's DPDP Act, and that it affects eligibility for large infrastructure projects with stringent IT and governance requirements.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Ramky Infrastructure operates through two broad business models: an EPC business that undertakes infrastructure projects across water and wastewater, industrial infrastructure, urban solutions, buildings and other infrastructure segments, spanning project planning, engineering, procurement, construction, commissioning and execution management; and a Developer and Infrastructure Solutions business that participates in development and public-private-partnership projects including industrial parks, water and wastewater infrastructure, transportation assets and urban infrastructure. Its customers are predominantly government authorities and related public-sector agencies, and its capabilities span EPC, Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM), PPP and Operation & Maintenance delivery models. This combination allows Ramky to participate across different stages of the infrastructure lifecycle, from project development and construction to commissioning and long-term operations.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's infrastructure requirements are changing — rapid urbanisation, growing industrial activity, water stress and increasing environmental requirements are creating a larger need for sustainable infrastructure solutions, which the MD says positions Ramky to participate in this growth particularly in water, wastewater and environmental infrastructure
- Sustained public capital expenditure remains central to India's growth: the Union Budget 2025-26 provided ₹11.21 lakh crore for capital expenditure (3.1% of GDP) and effective capital expenditure of ₹15.48 lakh crore (4.3% of GDP), with government capital outlay up nearly 89% from ₹5.92 lakh crore in FY2021-22
- Real GDP is estimated to grow 7.4% in FY2025-26 and construction GVA 7.8%, per the First Advance Estimates of the National Statistical Office
- The infrastructure opportunity is shifting from creating basic infrastructure to improving quality, capacity and efficiency of existing systems, and increasingly toward projects that combine construction with long-term operation, maintenance, resource efficiency and measurable outcomes — a structure that favours Ramky's EPC-plus-O&M model
- Water and wastewater demand driver: India generates approximately 112 billion litres of domestic and industrial wastewater daily, the world's third-largest, with urban areas about two-thirds of the volume and only 28% of urban wastewater currently treated
- Reuse of treated water for industrial cooling, construction and landscaping is estimated by the Economic Survey to represent an economic opportunity of ₹2.4-3.2 lakh crore by 2047, with the sector moving toward reuse, resource recovery, pollution control and circular water management
- Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0, approved in March 2026, extends the mission to December 2028 with an enhanced outlay of ₹8.69 lakh crore, emphasising reliable and sustainable drinking-water services; AMRUT 2.0 continues to support urban water supply, sewerage, septage management and water-body rejuvenation
- Performance-linked models such as Hybrid Annuity Models for sewage treatment are supporting the transition and align with Ramky's HAM capability
- Industrial parks: the sector grew 8.4% in the first half of FY2025-26; the Government's BHAVYA scheme approved in March 2026 provides for 100 plug-and-play industrial parks with ready infrastructure, driving demand for supporting utilities, water supply, wastewater treatment and common facilities
- Roads, bridges and transportation infrastructure continues to benefit from sustained public investment aimed at improving connectivity and reducing logistics costs
- PM GatiShakti continues to improve integrated planning and coordination across infrastructure projects, while continued EPC, PPP and hybrid-model private investment is creating new opportunities across transportation, urban infrastructure, water and industrial development
- The CFO states the Company enters the new financial year with real momentum and a business pipeline stronger than it has ever been
- The CFO states the order book stands at approximately INR 13,000 Crores, describing it as a signal of continued client trust
- FY26 wins cited as milestones: the INR 2,085 Crore water transmission project awarded by the Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board; the INR 1,401 Crore infrastructure works at Dighi Port Industrial Area awarded by Maharashtra Industrial Township Limited; and the INR 3,000 Crore Life Sciences City project awarded by the Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation
- The BRSR director's statement describes significant business momentum with several project wins across the EPC and developer portfolio, including HMWSSB Water Transmission in Telangana, Dighi Port Industrial Area Phase I in Maharashtra (MITL) and the 1,000-hectare Life Sciences park from MIDC

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Ramky's FY26 expansion is order-book driven rather than plant-capex driven: the Company added three large awards across its EPC and developer portfolio — a water transmission project from the Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board, the Dighi Port Industrial Area Phase 1 (Package A) infrastructure works from Maharashtra Industrial Township Limited, and a Life Sciences City project from the Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation. The Dighi Port Phase 1 award is an EPC contract for design, construction, testing, commissioning, operation and maintenance of infrastructure works under the Delhi Mumbai Industrial Corridor, with an awarded contract value of ₹1,400 crore, a 930-day construction period spanning five milestones from design to completion, and a four-year defect liability period. Alongside it, Ramky and MIDC are developing MILéS City, a 1,000-hectare integrated life sciences ecosystem in the Dighi Port Industrial Area comprising a 607.70 ha industrial zone, 125.54 ha of green spaces, 113.12 ha of roads and parking, 62.62 ha of common amenities, 51.33 ha of utilities and a 39.69 ha commercial zone, planned with an all-weather road network, GIS substation and power distribution, a common effluent treatment plant with ZLD facility, a dedicated co-generation power plant with steam distribution, hazardous waste management, a water treatment plant with distribution network, warehousing, an integrated command control centre and R&D, skill-development and emergency-response facilities. In water, the Godavari Drinking Water Supply Scheme Phase II & III Package II is being executed under the Hybrid Annuity Model over a two-year construction period followed by ten years of operation and maintenance, and comprises 65 km of 2,200 mm-dia raw-water main from Ghanpur to Osmansagar and Himayatsagar, 42 km of 2,400 mm-dia clear-water main from Ghanpur to Muthangi, water treatment plants of 120 MLD at Osmansagar and 70 MLD at Himayatsagar, and master balancing reservoirs of 102.5 ML combined capacity at Ghanpur and Golden Mile, supporting Hyderabad's water infrastructure and the Musi River rejuvenation. At V.O. Chidambaranar Port a Ramky JV is developing a 3 MLD seawater reverse-osmosis desalination plant on a Design-Build-Operate model with a 450 mm seawater intake pipeline and a 250 mm discharge pipeline, with the JV responsible for five years of operation and maintenance after commissioning. Structurally, the Company also consolidated its group: the NCLT Hyderabad Bench-II order dated 25 February 2026 approved the amalgamation of Sehore Kosmi Tollways Limited and Ramky Elsamex Hyderabad Ring Road Limited into Ramky Infrastructure Limited, and the assets and liabilities of the transferor companies have been vested in the Company. Management states it is also evaluating strategic partnerships and acquisitions that can add capabilities and expand the portfolio.
